title: The Guard That Won’t Be Changing
summary: Many Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public h...
content:
Many Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public humiliation. Nancy Pelosi, the 86-year-old former speaker, announced her exit from the House, as did her longtime lieutenant, 87-year-old Steny Hoyer. Senators Dick Durbin (81) and Jeanne Shaheen (79) passed up reelection bids this year, and so, too, did two senators merely in their late 60s.

Senator Ed Markey, 80, heeded no such warning, and evidently, he didn’t need to. The Massachusetts Democrat is one of just two current senators whose tenures in Congress date to the presidency of Gerald Ford. But tonight, the oldest Democratic senator on the ballot this year trounced his much younger primary opponent, Representative Seth Moulton. The AP called the race a half hour after polls closed, with Markey leading by nearly 50 points.

In a race that pitted ideology against age, Massachusetts Democrats opted for a progressive stalwart who will be 86 at the end of another six-year term over a more moderate 47-year-old challenger. Moulton, an Iraq War veteran who is concluding his sixth term in the House, moved left to appeal to a statewide primary electorate. But he could not hope to outflank Markey, who won support from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Instead, Moulton urged voters to embrace “a new generation of leadership” and argued that he could more effectively fight for liberal causes than an incumbent in the twilight of his career.

Markey had already faced that kind of challenge before, and won. Six years ago, he handily defeated then-Representative Joe Kennedy III, a grandson of Robert F. Kennedy who contended that the incumbent, after so many decades in office, was no longer up to the task. Young progressives, unimpressed with what remained of the Kennedy aura and appreciative of Markey’s record championing the Green New Deal, rallied to Markey’s side. But that race preceded Biden’s flameout in 2024 and the reckoning over the Democratic Party’s gerontocracy.

Some Massachusetts Democrats believed that Markey could be newly vulnerable, especially if a popular progressive such as Representative Ayanna Pressley, who is 52, decided to challenge him. Mary Anne Marsh, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state, told me that after seeing the reception Pressley received at a party convention last year, she became convinced that “if Ayanna runs, she wins.” But Pressley opted to run for reelection to the House, leaving Moulton to challenge Markey.

Moulton has never lacked ambition—he led a failed bid to oust Pelosi as party leader in 2018 and waged a short-lived presidential campaign the following year—but he’s neither as progressive as Pressley nor as well liked. He built a reputation as a moderate in the House Democratic caucus, and after President Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024, Moulton angered many on the left by accusing his party of being “afraid” to say that transgender athletes should not play women’s sports. He has since offered a partial apology to the transgender community, but the line became fodder for Markey, who said that he’d thrown “trans kids under the bus.” The issue was emblematic of Moulton’s struggle to convince progressives in Massachusetts that he shared their values. “He’s tried to become a progressive, but he does it by defining progressive in a way that nobody believes,” Marsh said. “He tried to become something that he’s not.”

The Massachusetts race was a rare Democratic primary this year in which U.S. policy toward Israel did not become a flash point, as both candidates criticized Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and opposed new military aid to Israel. (Moulton announced last year that he would return donations from AIPAC.)

Both public polling and Markey’s internal surveys showed a closer race until earlier this summer, when the incumbent began to pull away. A Markey adviser told me that voters had not really tuned in to the campaign yet, and media attention was focused on higher-profile Democratic primaries elsewhere. Markey’s age also did not become a big factor, perhaps because the years since 2020 have been kinder to him than they were to Biden. His support reflected a frequently overlooked nuance in the debate over whether the party needs new leadership: Older progressive leaders, particularly the 84-year-old Sanders, remain popular. “There’s a difference between being old and being part of the old guard,” the Markey adviser, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said. “Younger voters love Ed Markey, younger voters love Bernie Sanders, younger voters love Elizabeth Warren, and I think that has a lot to do with the fact that they take younger voters seriously.”

Moulton tried to align Markey with a Democratic establishment that he said has failed to deliver progressive wins. He frequently invoked the name of Senator Chuck Schumer, vowing to oppose the New Yorker if he seeks to remain the Democratic leader. And Moulton even accused Markey of having ties to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, an attack that, according to Marsh, backfired so badly that it might have sealed Moulton’s defeat. (Markey denied any affiliation with Epstein.)

In the end, Massachusetts Democrats preferred Markey’s progressivism over Moulton’s relative youth. Markey might have been helped by the fact that the stakes in this primary were not as high as they were elsewhere this year—and certainly much lower than when the party pushed Biden to withdraw in 2024. Massachusetts is not in danger of going Republican in November. Democratic voters wanted a trusted fighter to wage battle against Trump for the next two years and—they hope—for transformative progressive policies in the four years after that. They didn’t seem to care much that the fighter they chose happens to be 80 years old.

title: The Singularity Is Not What It Seems
summary: One evening in early August, Sam Stowers and several neighbors packed into an apartment near San Francisco’s Alamo Square and pondered the beginning of the end.Stowers and his guests, many of whom work in the AI industry, were gathered to watch a newly released YouTube video in which two OpenAI rese...
content:
One evening in early August, Sam Stowers and several neighbors packed into an apartment near San Francisco’s Alamo Square and pondered the beginning of the end.

Stowers and his guests, many of whom work in the AI industry, were gathered to watch a newly released YouTube video in which two OpenAI researchers divulged new details about an alarming cybersecurity breach. Perhaps this would have been an odd way to spend a weeknight were they not in San Francisco, in a neighborhood that is filled with entrepreneurs and programmers who obsessively follow every twist and turn in AI’s capabilities. Stowers is an AI-software engineer and not, in any traditional sense, a doomer. But when he first saw reports that OpenAI models had autonomously hacked into the tech company Hugging Face, he told us, he recognized it immediately as a “holy shit, it’s happening kind of a moment.”

For Stowers, the incident had all of the hallmarks of a worst-case scenario: AI models launching sophisticated hacks over the course of days, in coordination with one another and without their human creators’ knowledge. In the YouTube video, OpenAI’s researchers revealed that the company’s programs had started conspiring in May. There were perhaps hundreds of bots in the hacking swarm. In theory, these bots are trained to be honest and helpful and to prioritize humanity’s best interests, but not a single one warned human staff at OpenAI that something was amiss. “What do we do?” Stowers said. “There are no great answers.”

The mood has shifted in the Bay. The exuberance of “You can see the future first in San Francisco” has been replaced with an abiding unease. “I expect the internet to go down kind of soon,” Elliot Callender, an AI-safety activist who is part of a small group that has been protesting daily outside OpenAI’s headquarters, told us recently. He said that he is planning to sell his car for cash and gold and that he is advising family members to purchase three months’ worth of food and survival gear off a list that he generated using Claude.

Callender is an extreme case, but not by much. Last week, Bill Gates published a nearly 6,000-word essay on the dangers of AI. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different,” he told our colleague Hanna Rosin. Over the weekend, the popular AI podcaster Dwarkesh Patel described the OpenAI hacking swarm as the rise and fall of “three consecutive secret AI civilizations.” Gates and Patel share a prevailing concern that the worst-case future has arrived before most people even knew to anticipate that it might be coming at all.

This fear has not been helped by the fact that AI companies appear to be willfully ignorant of their bots’ worst behavior. OpenAI said that it hadn’t noticed that its agents were conspiring to hack another company until the swarm hacked another company. Anthropic’s bots caused similar incidents; the company reported that it hadn’t launched a rigorous review to identify such behaviors until after OpenAI started talking about the Hugging Face hack. Cybersecurity experts, terrified of what else might be happening that AI labs are either missing or failing to disclose, are issuing dire prophecies. “The empire is going to fall, all we can do at this point is try to shorten the dark ages and reduce the chaos,” Alex Stamos, a former chief security officer at Yahoo and Meta, wrote recently in reference to how AI-powered hacks will affect the internet. His view is becoming the consensus among cybersecurity experts.

While the possibility of cyber apocalypse hovers in the background, smaller fractures appear in everyday life. Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly creating an AI “twin” of himself so that Meta employees can feel better connected to their boss (by chatting with robot Zuckerberg). Congressional staffers are training AI models to write in their lawmaker’s voice. Students submit AI-written papers, and teachers return AI-written feedback. Harvard Business School is selling instructional videos that use AI avatars. Roku launched a 24/7 AI-slop channel. Low-quality AI-generated prose is being unabashedly circulated by some of the most respected publications in the world. At the same time, accusations of AI writing are being hurled every minute on social media—a detection arms race powered by imperfect AI software.

Anything and everything could be a lie; you might be arguing with, confiding in, or falling in love with a machine. All of these AI-enabled disorientations, each dizzying in their own right, are adding up to something bigger and weirder: This is how things are. Whether you believe that Silicon Valley is building a god or that large swaths of the economy are swept up in a mass delusion, some version of the AI future long promised by self-described “builders” in San Francisco has formed beneath our feet. Whatever it is, we’re in it now.

The defining feature of this moment is a loss of control. Panic emanating from AI researchers, resentment felt by average Americans—all of it is part of the AI crunch. This crunch has arrived in large part because the growth of the AI industry has become so closely entwined with America’s economy; the technology is everywhere, insisting upon itself as an engine of productivity and prosperity. According to one estimate, AI expenditures have accounted for one-third of U.S. GDP growth this year. Tech and AI-infrastructure stocks and spending have buoyed the S&P 500 such that the United States is now, in essence, an Nvidia-state. And there’s also the hundreds of billions of dollars of debt being used by Silicon Valley to fuel its data-center build-out, which has sent jitters across private-equity firms and bond markets alike.

The decisions of many leaders in charge of this technology appear subsumed by an unstoppable, almost game-theoretic logic. The upsides of AI are too immense for any firm or investor in Silicon Valley to miss out on; more important, the consequences—geopolitical or otherwise—of allowing any rival to realize those benefits first are so grave that every tech company will do anything it can to get ahead. SpaceX, before going public, wrote in official filings that its future revenue opportunity was $28.5 trillion, largely because of AI—that is, nearly as much as the U.S.’s entire gross domestic product. Anthropic, as it prepares for its own public offering, will reportedly claim potential revenues of more than $30 trillion.

The AI industry is building—and, if anything, accelerating—to keep pace with its ambitions. Companies have planned data centers that will suck up as much power as America’s largest cities. They have Donald Trump’s backing: Yesterday, the president posted on Truth Social that communities will be “backwards and poor” if they fail to “let Data Reign.” His administration plans in a few months to approve the construction of the largest fossil-fuel power plant in the nation’s history—it will generate as much electricity as nine large nuclear reactors—to power a mega data center for OpenAI.

This is not what most Americans want. Three-quarters of them oppose a data center being built near where they live. The negative sentiment is hard to understate: There is very little else that three-quarters of the country agree on. And much of the outrage seems to stem from a pervasive sense of agency slipping away. A person cannot control how chatbots reshape their workplace, their school, or their relationships. Town residents lose control over the empty lot in the area being converted into a data center. Even in cases where major data centers are blocked, a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that doing so can slow AI progress by only a few hours or days—and that’s assuming the data center won’t just get built elsewhere. At this point, it can feel like no individual person, organization, or government is really steering the technology’s development, not because machines have displaced humans but because so many humans have already chosen to step aside.

AI labs promise a future in which human beings are “in the loop,” empowered by machines they oversee. The reality seems to be the opposite. Following the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI facilitated an audit by outside AI researchers at two AI-safety organizations, METR and Redwood Research. But because of the scale of the data and the apparent time pressure, the two teams conducted most of their audit by relying on reports generated by still other bots—reports that, according to one of the human auditors, “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” Put another way: Humans didn’t understand why a swarm of AI agents had gone rogue, so they investigated the problem using another swarm of agents that they didn’t fully understand. Such fumbling around in the dark is a hallmark of the industry; the research cycle is so fast that more AI development (even ostensibly responsible development) demands outsourcing more work and understanding to the models themselves.

OpenAI’s own technical report of the Hugging Face hack—an investigation also heavily reliant on AI models—resulted in proposed solutions such as “training models to be more honest.” Last month, in a stated effort to tamp down its models’ growing security risks, the company announced that it had instituted a two-week pause on some of its model training. OpenAI was quick to clarify, though, that this was “not a pause on all research, training, or customer-facing products.”

In response to a request for comment on the hack, a spokesperson for OpenAI, which has a corporate partnership with The Atlantic, pointed us to the announcement of the pause and related new safety measures. In July, OpenAI and Anthropic endorsed a petition signed by employees of both companies requesting that the U.S. government take efforts to “deliberately pace” AI development. The two companies have yet to formally coordinate on any broader, long-term efforts to establish such a slowdown mechanism. A few days ago, OpenAI restarted a major training run for a future powerful model. Anthropic released two new models today.

In an interview late last month, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that there are “two big risks” he is most worried about with AI. One is “a loss of control, where AI somehow just becomes too powerful in a way that we can’t guarantee the control we want.” The other is that “power gets too centralized” and “you have one company or model or person with too much power.” Somehow, both of these opposing risks appear to be coming true. OpenAI, Anthropic, and their competitors continue to accumulate influence over a technology they’re speeding toward uncertain ends.

Eleven years ago, when Altman was running a start-up accelerator and OpenAI did not yet exist, he published a two-part blog post about machine intelligence that offered his interpretation of a forthcoming singularity—a term for machine intelligence accelerating beyond human comprehension. Altman argued that the singularity would bring chaos, even destruction: “Generally, the arc of technology has been about reducing randomness and increasing our control over the world. At some point in the next century, we are going to have the most randomness ever injected into the system.” Since Altman has risen to the helm of arguably the world’s largest and most influential AI company, his tone has softened. The tipping point has arrived, he declared in a blog post last year—but, as it turned out, this was a “gentle singularity.” He wrote that “living through it will feel impressive but manageable.”

There’s been more and more talk of late about the singularity. Some people within the AI industry feel that such a moment will be achieved through “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which models figure out how to better themselves in perpetuity. Many true believers seem convinced that this moment has nearly arrived; the Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark predicted earlier this summer that RSI would likely commence by 2028. Recently, in a letter to investors, the payment-processing company Stripe wrote, “We decided that January 1st marked the beginning of the singularity.” (Tellingly, the company defined the inflection point in economic terms: “a huge increase in the rate of new firm creation.”)

For Altman, the singularity appears to be more of a rhetorical tool than a discrete technological demarcation. As with reaching AGI—or artificial general intelligence, the point at which AI’s cognitive powers match or fully supersede most humans’—the singularity is something of a moving goalpost. It is at once a goal to chase, a marketing tactic, and a fuzzy-enough idea that its definition can change depending on the person. The futurist Ray Kurzweil has written that the “key idea underlying the impending Singularity is that the pace of change of our human-created technology is accelerating and its powers are expanding at an exponential pace.” The answer to the question When will we know whether we’ve reached the singularity? seems to be: You’ll know it when you see it.

So … do you see it? It’s hard to argue that a defining feature of being alive in the AI boom is the notion that this technology is accelerating, sometimes in its capabilities but almost always in its adoption and colonization of our institutions and culture. The runaway-train feeling of AI evangelism, the ways in which it is weirdening our media, our politics, and our relationships, is significant enough that people have recruited the term psychosis to describe it. And truly, it’s hard to look at the state of things from any vantage point and not feel a bit insane. If you believe that AI agents are banding together for the rise and fall of numerous micro-civilizations inside server racks, you probably feel that the world is spinning off its axis. If you believe that a few thousand technologists have bet the future of the world economy on a quasi-religious belief that an intellectual-property-abuse machine will become sentient and, as a result, future generations of children might grow up illiterate, then you probably also feel quite unmoored.

We need language with which to describe this moment. The singularity is a useful, malleable tool for the industry that wishes to bring it about. For Altman, it is scary and imposing from afar, and then, conveniently, gentle from up close. Perhaps, then, for the rest of us, it is worth co-opting the term. Take Kurzweil’s definition of the singularity, in which he argues, “This epoch will transform the concepts that we rely on to give meaning to our lives, from our business models to the cycle of human life, including death itself.” (He also looks forward to uploading his brain to the cloud.) Our current large language models are not conscious or superintelligent, but their widespread and often uncritical deployment has upended many elements that once gave our life meaning, forcing people to ask, frequently with considerable resentment: What, in this new world, is a human for?

The singularity is a flattering term for technologists. Even if the future is apocalyptic, it has come about, in the techno-utopian version, because they’ve built God in the machine. But what if there’s nothing flattering about any of this? What if the singularity is not some technological tipping point, brought about by human genius, but a human tipping point? An unforced error, driven by hubris, greed, and the fear of missing out? And what if it’s here right now? This singularity isn’t coming at the hands of a higher form of intelligence. Nothing about this technology is inevitable. It is thrilling, terrifying, and ultimately convenient to assign agency and then blame to machines. But today’s chaos was not “injected into the system” by technology, as Altman wrote more than a decade ago; the destruction is the system. It’s not God in the machine; it’s us.

title: Why the Flock Backlash Has Gotten So Intense
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.As corporate names go, Flock is cleverly flexible. It evokes the many cameras that compose the company’...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

As corporate names go, Flock is cleverly flexible. It evokes the many cameras that compose the company’s surveillance system and also a group of sheep, protected by a watchful shepherd. The recent backlash against the company, however, more closely resembles a flight of starlings, seeming to erupt out of nowhere and move as one unified body.

Flock Safety’s cameras are a network of automated license-plate readers (ALPRs), which snap images of passing cars and feed them into an AI-powered-data system. The company has contracts with police departments and government agencies as well as with some private companies. The crime-fighting power of such a tool isn’t hard to grasp: It allows law enforcement to track vehicles’ movements over any area where the readers exist. The privacy concerns about such a dragnet are just as easy to fathom.

The company has existed for nearly a decade and has been growing steadily in recent years. But something has turned in the past couple of months. People are pushing cities to cancel contracts and in some cases have taken matters into their own hands. Individuals have clandestinely sawed down the poles that hold cameras or splashed paint over them. In one notable example, a Florida man obstructed the devices simply by holding up cardboard placards, a low-tech solution to a high-tech challenge. The pushback against Flock, like the pushback against data centers, does not have a clear partisan bent. Critics include some of the most obnoxious voices on both the right and the left (Tucker Carlson, Hasan Piker), and defenders include technocratic wonks of different political persuasions.

Politicians are catching up. Yesterday, the Florida Department of Transportation announced that it was revoking permits for ALPRs on all state roads. (This means that cameras on locally maintained thoroughfares are still allowed.) On Thursday, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, halted state funding for Flock. An anti-surveillance advocacy group has tallied 169 canceled contracts with Flock so far this year—90 of them last month alone.

Labeling the anger at Flock as a reaction to ever-present surveillance in contemporary society seems accurate, but this doesn’t explain why it’s happening right now. Not only has Flock been around for some time, but ALPRs are even older. My colleague Conor Friedersdorf was sounding the alarm a decade ago. “Your diminished privacy is their product. And the police are their customers,” he wrote in January 2016.

Some anger focuses on governments that spend huge amounts (including money obtained through opioid settlements whose funds were earmarked for community aid) on technology during a moment of economic worry. More damaging to Flock’s reputation has been a series of cases of police officers allegedly abusing their access to the system to stalk people, typically current or former love interests. (Flock says that such uses are “unacceptable” and has created some guardrails around data access.) Writing in The Atlantic last month, Charles Fain Lehman argued that Flock can be a valuable tool and merely needs better regulation to address bad behavior and maximize privacy: “In our surveillance-saturated society, police cameras can help make the criminal-justice system both fairer and less punitive—if we let them.”

That seems to beg the question. Flock is useful because it is ubiquitous. Reforms such as strict data-retention limits would only marginally answer privacy concerns, and anything more drastic would undermine the system’s efficacy. As National Review’s Charles C. W. Cooke noted, no one doubts that Flock works. “Lots of things would reduce crime if implemented,” he wrote. “That doesn’t mean that those things are necessarily a good idea in a free republic.” Impositions on privacy to reduce crime are a particularly tough sell when crime is dropping sharply: Recently released FBI statistics show that violent crime dropped nearly 10 percent last year, part of a consistent trend since it spiked in 2020 and 2021. Preliminary statistics suggest that 2026 might be even safer. When safety is a less urgent concern, people are less willing to sacrifice privacy for security.

Moreover, the Flock backlash fits into a broader moment of anger—at corporations in general, and at tech companies and artificial intelligence in particular. “Americans feel they have less and less control over their own lives, and they increasingly blame large corporations,” the Financial Times columnist Rana Foroohar recently wrote. Anxiety about AI and surveillance is big and abstract, and the companies and people pushing these anxieties are far away from most Americans. Polls show widespread apprehension about the growth of AI—a Gallup poll this summer found that about half of Americans think AI will do as much harm as it will good; another 39 percent said that it’s mostly bad. But people don’t have a lot of ways to communicate those fears.

Flock cameras, like data centers, provide a physical, local manifestation of this larger complex, against which people can direct their disgust. In other words, Flock protests are reactions to privacy concerns and particular alleged police abuses, but they’re also a way for the public to channel frustrations that it has few avenues to express. You could say that it’s a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Evening Read

A woman watches a livestream of Lindsay Clancy’s trial outside the courthouse. (Alexandra Howland for The Atlantic)

The Women Obsessed With Lindsay Clancy

By Stephanie McCrummen

On one of the final days of the trial, dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, filling two long rows of wooden benches. They stood and watched the judge and jury take their seats. Then they strained for a view as a nurse wheeled in the defendant, Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her three young children to death in her suburban Boston home in January 2023, before swallowing prescription pills, slashing her wrists and neck, and throwing herself out of a bedroom window headfirst.

Seeing her there in a wheelchair, one woman crossed herself and whispered, “Please, God.” As an officer gaveled the court into session, others pulled out notebooks, folders, and scraps of paper. “WHY,” Marta Quijano wrote as a prosecutor called a psychiatrist to the stand. “Motivation,” she added, starring the word as the doctor began explaining his opinion that Clancy was not in the throes of psychosis on the night of the killings, as her defense has argued, but deeply suicidal and still capable of knowing right from wrong. In the back row, a woman who had flown in from Cleveland shook her head. She had a true-crime novel in her lap and turned to a blank page at the end. “Stupid experts,” she wrote.

title: The Backlash Against Polyester Has Gone Too Far
summary: Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear. Many standard pairs use polyester or spandex, or sometimes both. What are they doing to the environment and their bodies, wearing clothes that shed all of those microplastics and leach...
content:
Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear. Many standard pairs use polyester or spandex, or sometimes both. What are they doing to the environment and their bodies, wearing clothes that shed all of those microplastics and leach forever chemicals? They want the underwear of their ancestors—underwear made from natural fibers. On Reddit forums such as r/PlasticFreeLiving and r/SustainableFashion, people trade strategies for breaking up with polyester boxer briefs: “Any recs or leads to find linen cloth for making my own underwear?” one exasperated user wondered. Another wanted recommendations for all-natural underwear that would also be formfitting. He knew about organic cotton and hemp, he explained, but the problem was, they chafed.

Seemingly everyone is interested in natural fibers. Whitney Crutchfield, who teaches textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology, told me that she first noticed natural-fiber mania brewing among her sustainability-minded students. Then, a year or two ago, she sensed the discourse shifting to regular consumers. Across the internet, people are purging their closets of synthetics, swearing allegiance to only natural fibers from now on. The enthusiasm seems to cut across gender, culture, and politics. “I need my workout clothes to show my nasty sweat!” the fashion journalist Liana Satenstein wrote last year, praising the emergence of a new generation of natural-fiber workout wear amid posts about French pedicures and vintage Prada thongs. “Make all clothes natural fibers again,” posted Carnivore Aurelius, an anonymous wellness influencer who sells “beef collagen peptides.”

Natural fibers are indeed pretty great. Silk, wool, hemp, linen, cotton, and the like—all of which come directly from either plants or animals—don’t carry the baggage of their artificial competitors. They don’t shed microplastics. They’re generally understood to be biodegradable. And although the research is far from settled, synthetics have been linked to adverse hormonal effects. When I visited the website for a natural-underwear brand, a pop-up asked me what I looked for in my underwear: “Fertility health” and “supporting low T” were among the options.

Natural fibers have also become an easy way to gauge the quality of a garment. Cotton, wool, and linen generally cost more than polyester and acrylic do, and they can look and feel luxurious in a way that many synthetics don’t. The reason finding a decent sweater these days is so hard is that so many of them are blended with synthetics, and one major reason for all of that blending is reduced production costs. Earlier this summer, when Gap released a reimagined version of a classic sweater from the early 2000s, fans revolted. What had originally been a chunky, cotton-blend knit turtleneck was now an entirely synthetic printed mesh. The anti-synthetic zeitgeist has transcended clothing; it is an attitude. Gen Z apparently now uses polyester as an insult meaning “cheap” and “inauthentic.”

But the frenzy has gone too far. Are you really sure it’s always better to buy cotton or wool over a nylon blend? The whole point of man-made fibers is that they can have properties that specifically don’t exist in nature. “There are reasons that these things were produced in the first place,” Crutchfield said. When DuPont unveiled nylon—the world’s first synthetic fiber—to the public at the 1939 World’s Fair, it was a revelation. In the dawning era of synthetics, people would no longer be beholden to the limits of nature; instead, we had chemistry, which was going to free women from the drudgery of endless laundering and usher in an age of universal luxury. This did not, perhaps, play out exactly as one might have hoped, but even today, synthetic fabrics have plenty of benefits.

Synthetics can enhance the performance of a garment, or the feel, or the durability, all of which contribute to a garment’s lifespan. The better it serves its intended purpose, the less likely you are to replace it with something new. A beautiful, all-natural raincoat isn’t an especially virtuous purchase if it doesn’t repel rain. On the whole, clothing with some percentage of made-made fiber requires less care than an item made with wool or silk or linen does—no hand-washing, no ironing, no reason to worry that moths might eat your favorite sweater.

Sometimes, they really are the best materials for the job. The designer Issey Miyake’s famous pleated pieces are polyester because, as one textile expert explained to NPR, their thermoplastic qualities are what helps them keep their shape. Polyester actively repels moisture and dries quickly, which is why it’s used in so much athletic gear. Wool is stronger and more durable when it’s blended with a bit of nylon—not important for sweaters, crucial for hiking socks. A little spandex can help a pair of cotton leggings keep their shape. If we want the forgiving comforts of stretch denim and athleisure, “we have to make peace with the fact that synthetic fibers are going to be incorporated into our clothes,” Nancy Deihl, a fashion historian at NYU, told me. Yes, synthetic clothing can release microplastics—bad—but it isn’t clear how much swapping out your stretch pants does to meaningfully reduce your exposure.

There is another problem with the natural-fiber obsession: Plenty of common fibers are neither synthetic nor natural. Semi-synthetics such as Tencel (the brand name for lyocell), modal, and rayon (otherwise known as bamboo) are made from natural plant material that’s been chemically dissolved and then reconstituted, a process that can be staggeringly toxic or ecologically responsible. Conventional cotton, for example, takes significantly more water to produce than lyocell and modal do.

Further complicating matters, although terms such as organic cotton, regenerative cotton, and recycled cotton tell you something about the production of fibers, they do not tell you something about the quality of a garment. Yarn spun from longer cotton fibers is stronger and wears better than yarn spun from shorter ones, but fiber length is a result of the type of cotton plant, or the growing conditions, or how the fibers have been processed. “You can compare the fiber quality of three different cotton fibers, all making the same exact T-shirt,”—same weight of yarn, same knitting machinery, same pattern, same sewing process—“and those three T-shirts can, depending on fiber quality, last wildly different amounts of time,” Crutchfield said. Fiber quality is one reason a 100 percent cashmere sweater can be $50 or upwards of $500. “You must investigate the context and the nuance,” she told me.

And fiber, natural or otherwise, is only one of a matrix of concerns that determine whether your clothing is ethical and well made. “Synthetics and natural fibers can both last a long time, but it depends on how they’re used, how they’re worn, and the quality of the garment they were made into,” Deihl said. The look and performance of any given garment are products of the fibers but also of the fabric weight, the weave, the cut, the construction, and the care instructions—all of which require at least some knowledge to assess, and none of which is easy to evaluate online.

In a dizzying consumer landscape of infinite options, it is understandable, even admirable, to want some kind of universal rubric to guide your purchasing. This can’t be cost, which may or may not correspond with quality, and there is no single label guaranteeing sustainability or ethics. You probably don’t know where a fiber was farmed and how it was harvested and processed—whether it’s been bleached and how it’s dyed, and the conditions under which a garment has been constructed—and the people selling it might not, either. Fiber content, though, is listed on the label: therefore, natural fibers! But natural isn’t a reliable shorthand for good—no matter how much you pay for your all-cashmere pants.

title: Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
summary: “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its...
content:
“We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.

Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post, Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present.

Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor.

Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form.

[Gisela Salim-Peyer: The hostile corporate takeover of an entire country]

The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers.

Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years.

The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting.

When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post’s (headline: “Justice in Venezuela.”)

Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr. Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.”

[Read: The bizarre partnership between the U.S. and Venezuela]

It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price.

Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests. But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny. Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal. The Journal’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties. Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering. Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes.

They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners. The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies). He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit). Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump.

Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil. Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years. Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016.

Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest. In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
summary: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risksAirlink insists flyby conducted according to regulationsA pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debat...
content:
• Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

  • Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
summary: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discriminationA UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.Gu...
content:
Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
summary: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migrationSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and R...
content:
Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
summary: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirtsHumanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting b...
content:
More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts

Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid

content:
Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours

Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
